**KLADA — a village in no parish table, no gazetteer, and no person's record.** **Marijan Vukelić**, born **27 January 1894** at *«Klada-senj»* — the coast below Sveta Jelena — wife **Rosie** b.1896, children **Walter** 1922, **Catherine** 1925, **John** 1927, Brooklyn, **five filings 1935–1948**. **The same shape as Sinac this morning, found the same way.** And Vukelić is not a stranger's name: it is the line **Milka Papić married into**, and this archive records **no Vukelić emigration at all**.

**Three more, all confirmed.** **Miro Šojat** (*Sojath*), b. **5 Nov 1910** at **Senj**, Astoria NY 1955 — Šojat runs from Marija Šojat of Krivi Put to the Nikola Šojat on the Senj stone, and none of them has an emigration recorded. **Luka Orsanich** — *Orešković*, **ahnentafel 21's surname** — b. **15 Oct 1897** at **Otočac**, the Bronx 1931. And **Kate Žubrinić**, b. **27 Oct 1895**, born at **Otočac**: the archive knew her husband was, **it did not know she was**.

**Two sworn records of one family, and not one child's date agrees.** Ivan and Kate filed separately and both were sworn: George **7 Jan 1923** / **21 May 1922**; Joseph 8 Feb / **2** Feb 1924; John **13 Nov** / **8 Oct** 1932. Kate's own birth year is **1905** in his 1936 filing and **1895** in his 1939 one. **The most formal record this family left in America is not reliable to the month.** Excellent for *who* and *where*; no better than a manifest for *when*.

Written up in `sources/findmypast/naturalisations-2026-09-16.md`.

---

**The surname box matches EXACTLY, and that is the third form of the same lesson today.** Four of this archive's surnames returned **0** in the petitions — *kalanj*, *papic*, *sojat*, *spalj* — and **Miro Šojat is demonstrably in the set**. `lastname=sojat` **0**; `lastname=sojath` **4**. **A zero on a surname means «not under that spelling», never «not here».** (The *keywords* box is the opposite — fuzzy enough to return Greek names for *klada*.) Zubrinich/Zubrinic/Zubrinick/Zubrinec; Perpic/Prpic spelled differently **in one entry**; now Sojat/Sojath. **One letter, and the search is blind.**

**Kalanj is «Kalan» in America — and the Kalan family is Slovene.** `lastname=kalan` returns **20 petitions** the 143-record Kalanj harvest never saw, and it looked like the find of the afternoon. **Frank Kalan**, b. 10 April 1873, birthplace **«Krain, Austria»** — **Carniola, Slovenia, not Lika**. *Kalan* is a Slovene surname in its own right, not a rendering of Kalanj. **Recorded so nobody spends a day on it.** Same for the second Vukelić household: **Louis Peter Vukelić**, b.1892, birthplace **«Rogul»**, New Haven 1926 — not Klada, not Senj, no relation established.

**And Brinje is confirmed as an emigration source, in the clerks' own spelling.** **Vid Peter Karakas**, b. **26 September 1920**, birthplace **«Brinje Plasca, Yugoslavia»** — **Brinje AND Plašćica in one field.** The trial found seven Kalanj manifests giving *«Brinje, Plaščica, Kurjak and Velgovica»*; here is the same pairing thirty years later in a different record type. Karakaš is not one of this archive's surnames, but **the form the clerks wrote is** — and [row 50](/worklist/) wants exactly that.

**Where the villages stand:** Otočac **7**, Senj **12**, Brinje **1** (fuzzy); Karlobag, Novi Vinodolski, Jurjevo, Selce **0**; Ledenice only a Czech *Karel Tuma*. **The seam is inland and it is Otočac.** The coastal parishes this archive has read most sent nobody to New York under a searchable spelling.

---

**All nineteen filings read: fourteen people, and thirteen of them went to New York.** `sources/findmypast/senj-otocac-naturalisations.psv` is the register — twelve Senj filings and seven Otočac ones resolving to **six and seven people**, plus Brinje's one. Brooklyn, the Bronx, Astoria, Jackson Heights, Long Island City, Tarrytown, Nassau. Only **Mike Mukulino**, the oldest, born **1858**, went elsewhere — to **Boston**.

**That is a third diaspora, and it touches neither of the two this archive already had.** The Žubrinići of **Prozor** went to **Port Pirie** and became moulders in a lead smelter. The **Kalanji** of Klenovica went to **Leadville, Colorado** and the Michigan copper country. **Senj and Otočac went to New York.**

**And «Birth country» turns out not to be evidence.** The same town, by American clerks: *Senj, Hungary* (1920) · *Senj, Austria* (1928) · *Senj, Hrvatska, Austria* (1924) · *Senj, Yugoslavia* (1928) · *Senj, Jugoslavia* (1955). **Rukavina and Hammerschmidt filed in the SAME YEAR, 1928, about the SAME TOWN, and called it two different countries.** It is neither the empire at birth nor the empire at filing — **it is what the man in front of the clerk said**. The transcribed birth PLACE is the evidence; the birth country is not.

**Five of the fourteen are inside a filmed register, to the day.** Otočac births are filmed **1834–1858** and all seven Otočac people were born 1888–1917, so **not one is reachable**. Senj births are filmed **1734–1894**, which puts **Mukulino (1858), Rukavina (1886), Grzin (1888)** and both 1894 men — **Vukelić and Hammerschmidt** — in range.

**Marijan Vukelić is the one to open first**: born **27 January 1894**, the surname **Milka Papić married into**, and a birthplace — **Klada** — this archive has never had.

---

**Every search run is now written down — `sources/findmypast/probes-2026-09-16.psv`, 59 of them, 29 of which are zeros.** A zero costs the same as a find to obtain and nothing to repeat, and the trial recorded its negatives for the same reason.

**The archive's other surnames are all clean negatives in the petitions.** *Papich* 13 — Rudolph b.1885 was **born in Italy**, Stojan's oath gives no town. *Blazevich* 6 — Alice b.1894 was **born in Russia**. *Boras* 16 — Irene b.1884 was **born in Budapest**, James b.1886 in **Greece**. *Prpich*, *perpich*, *papic*, *vukelich*, *kalanj* all **0**. **The only archive surnames in this record set are Vukelić (Klada), Šojat (Senj) and Orešković (Otočac)** — and all three were found by searching the **place**, not the name.

**And the village seam is exhausted.** *Gospić* 1 (not our surname), *Smiljan* 0, *Karlobag* 0 — **the best-read parish in this archive sent nobody** — *Novi Vinodolski*, *Jurjevo*, *Selce*, *Prozor* all 0; *Ledenice* two filings by a Czech; *Povile* twenty «Povill»s; *Fiume* **516**, a city and overwhelmingly Italian. **Otočac and Senj are the only two that yield**, and both have now been read out in full.

**Published**: `/america` gained the third stream, the fourteen-person table with per-person reachability, and the «birth country is not evidence» section. `tools/emigrants.py` builds it from the PSV so the counts cannot drift.

---

**17 September 2026 — the birthplace sweep, run through the villages the 16th did not reach.** Same method, which is the only one on this site that works: the **naturalisation petitions are the one record set where the birth place is INDEXED**, so they can be searched by *where somebody came from* rather than by what they were called. Every non-zero below was confirmed by opening the transcript and reading **«Birth place as transcribed»**; nothing is taken from a results list.

**Nine zeros, and they are worth as much as the finds** because they need never be repeated: **Krivi Put, Smokvica, Krmpote, Sinac, Kompolje, Bribir, Sveti Juraj, Mrzli Dol** — and that includes **the two villages this family actually came from**. Nobody filed a petition in the Southern District of New York from Smokvica Krmpotska or from Krivi Put. The Senj emigration went to New York; the Blažević and Prpić emigration, if there was one, did not.

**Three households came out, from three villages this file had never held:**

* **KLENOVICA — Frank Pavelić, born 2 April 1894**, wife Pauline b. 25 January 1903, children Frank 1921 and Pauline 1923, the Bronx. **Klenovica is the Kalanj village**, and the one man who filed from it is not a Kalanj. He is also entered under **two surnames three years apart** — *Pavelich* on the 1939 petition, **PAELICK** on the 1936 declaration — same birth date, same wife, same two children. That is the Žubrinić lesson again: **the spelling that finds a family is the one the American clerk wrote**, and an exact-match surname box will never return both halves of one man.
* **GRIŽANE — Kuzma Knez, born 25 September 1893**, entered as *«Belgrad, Grizane, Croatia Austria»*. **That is not a slip.** Belgrad is the other half of the municipality's own name — **Grižane-Belgrad** — so the clerk wrote the hamlet and then the parish, the same shape a house number takes in a register.
* **GRIŽANE — Mihovil Likarić, born 29 September 1885**, wife Katie, daughters Veronika 1920 and Anica 1921. **One impossibility, left as written**: Katie is indexed as born **25 January 1911**, which would make her a mother at nine. One of the two dates is wrong, this archive does not know which, and both are copied as the index has them.

**Four more villages returned candidates that are NOT confirmed** and are recorded as candidates: Crikvenica 4, Vrbnik 7, Brlog 4, Jablanac 2. **Lukovo's single hit is fuzzy noise** — the name is *Pietrzak*, which is Polish.

**And the URL form is written down now**, because it was not, and an hour went into finding it again: the search host serves the **form**, `www` serves the **results**, and the record set is selected by `datasetname` with the set's **exact printed name**. A guessed slug in the path gives 404 and a guessed display name gives 500. `sources/findmypast/probes-2026-09-16.psv`

---

**20 September 2026 — the set read by surname, now that the villages are exhausted. And the first thing it taught is that an index count is not a people count.**

`kalan` returns **20 rows** and holds **two households**. The rows are of three kinds and only one is worth opening:

| Row kind | What it gives |
|---|---|
| **Declaration / Petition** | birth date, **birth place as transcribed**, spouse, every child with a date |
| **Oath of allegiance** | a name, a year and a certificate number — **nothing else at all** |
| ids ending `/1 /2 /3 /4` | relations named *on* a record, not petitioners |

Four oaths were opened before the pattern was clear. **Skip them**; only `/0` is the applicant, and only a declaration or petition carries a birthplace.

**THE KALANJ LEAD IS DEAD, and that is worth as much as a find.** The trial's closing note recorded *«kalanj 0, kalan 20»* and left the twenty as a lead worth following. They are a **Slovene** family from **Krain** — Carniola — and a **Polish** family from **Rudnyki**:

* **Frank Kalan**, b. **10 April 1873**, *«Krain, Austria»*, wife Karoline b. 21 Aug 1883
* **Katherine Kalan**, b. **16 July 1893**, *«Rudnyki, Poland»*, husband Teodor

**Kalanj is the largest surname in the target list — 95 of the 386 — and the one record set on this site that indexes a birthplace holds not one of them.** Nobody from Klenovica or Brinje filed in these courts. That closes a line of enquiry rather than opening one, which is the whole reason the negatives are written down.

**And one new man.** **Louis Peter Vukelić, born 18 March 1892**, *«Rogul, Jugo-Slavia»*, wife Mary — **New Haven, Connecticut**, declared 1926 and sworn 1931. He is the third Vukelić in the set and the only one not already held: Marijan of **Klada-senj** is in New York, and this is a different man in a different state.

**«Rogul» is deliberately not resolved.** It is written the same way on both filings five years apart, so it is not a slip of one pen — but Ogulin and Rogulje have both been thought of here and neither is evidence. Guessing which Croatian place a clerk's spelling «must» be is exactly how this archive put a family on Krk for a week on the strength of a pencil annotation. It stands in the town column as transcribed.

**The sweep continued through the rest of the family's surnames, and they are other families.** `papich` (13 rows, 7 petitioners, **3 opened**) gives **Zara** — that is **Zadar**, in Dalmatia — and a *«Soldo or Papich»* household whose second surname is Herzegovinian. `blazevich` (6 rows, 3 petitioners) is **one** household, born at *«Rutkishki, Russia»*. Neither is Senj, neither is Smokvica. Four of the seven papich petitioners are **unopened, and recorded as unopened rather than as absent.**

---

**And a caution about the «birth country» column, found by accident and worth more than the searches that found it.**

**One man gives two different birth countries five years apart:**

| Filing | Name | Born | Birth country |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1919 declaration | Riedy Papich | 26 Mar 1885 | **«Zara, Austria»** |
| 1924 petition | Rudolph Papich | 26 Mar 1885 | **«Italy»** |

Same birth date, same Philadelphia court, consecutive record ids. **Zara is Zadar, and it passed from Austria to Italy at Rapallo in 1920 — between his two filings.** So *birth country* in this index is **the country that held the place when the clerk wrote, not when the person was born**, and the same man is findable under two nationalities depending which paper you open.

This archive already publishes [a sovereignty timeline](/frontier/) for exactly this reason — Anton Rudolf Defranceski *«was baptised under Austria, made an Italian subject at Rapallo without moving, and died under occupation»*. It now has an American index demonstrating the same thing against one man's own name, twice.

---

**The naturalisation set is now swept both ways, and it is exhausted.**

* **by village** — every parish and hamlet in this archive's gazetteer
* **by surname** — `kalan`, `vukelic`, `papich`, `blazevich`, `boras`, `borash`, `sojath`, `prpich`, `papic`

**Everything it holds for this family is already written down.** Every other hit belongs to somebody else — **Slovene** (Krain), **Polish** (Rudnyki), **Dalmatian** (Zara), **Herzegovinian** (Soldo), **Russian** (Rutkishki), **Hungarian** (Budapest), **Greek** (Skafers) and **Ashkenazi** (Sonken, Barchasch) families who happen to share a surname.

**And the names were not trusted to say so.** *«Max Sonken or Boras»* and *«Matie Borash or Barchasch»* look Ashkenazi; *«James Boras»* looks Croatian. **Judging by the look of a name is the mistake this archive keeps having to write down**, so three transcripts were opened: Budapest, **Skafers in Greece**, and an oath with no birth data at all. The Greek one is the point — **it is the record that looked most like ours and is not.** Boras is a Greek surname as well as a Croatian one.

**What that leaves of row 57 is the 386-name target list itself**, searched person by person with the given-name forms that [row 60](/worklist/) built — which is a long sitting rather than a sweep, and the sweeps are what is finished.

rows.what: /open-questions/ is rows now — and nothing was summarised in the move
rows.note:
**Done 17 September 2026.** 166 lines of hand-written prose, with the questions inlined as a `const` in the page, are now `site/src/data/questions.json` — **28 questions** in the shape `kit/components/Questions.astro` reads, which had been sitting unused because only two of the seven archives held their questions as data.

**The shape is the point.** A question is the question, **what is known**, **what has been tried**, and **the record that would answer it**. The middle field is the one most archives leave out and it is the one that stops a dead end being walked twice — so /open-questions/ now says, on the question about Casparus Žubrinić, that the status animarum was opened, read, and does **not** hold this family. That was in the prose; it was in the middle of nine hundred words.

**19 open, 9 answered**, filterable by state. Nineteen of the twenty-eight carry a «what has been tried».

**Nothing was summarised.** The split was checked word by word against the prose it replaced — every word of every old body and «what would settle it», against every word of the new four fields. The first pass dropped **313 word occurrences**, and two of those losses were real: the status animarum's own column list and what it was judged to cost, and the godparent column at Smokvica 114. Both were put back. What remains unmatched is **49 occurrences across 28 questions** — connectives, and verbs moved into the past tense because a thing that has been tried is no longer being tried.

| | |
|---|---|
| **state** | a civil register kept by a government — **1** |
| **register** | a parish register kept by a priest — **1** |
| **tree** | somebody's genealogy, however carefully made — **1** |
| **background** | history and statistics; true of a place, not of a person — **7** |
| **rejected** | consulted, and not relied on — **1** |
| **absent** | not consulted, and the page says so — **1** |

**There is no `kit/components/Sources.astro`** — the row named a component that does not exist, so the page renders the rows itself. The data is in the shape one would want, so adopting it is cheap if the kit ever grows one.

rows.what: Say Your Name — the archive was searching one form of a name out of eight
rows.note:
**Raised by a question, 17 September 2026:** *«are you searching all the variations of a name?»*

**For surnames, yes, and it had been proved** — `ZUBRINICH` returns 191 records, `ZUBRINIC` a different 119, `ZUBRINICK` ten more, one family. **For given names, no.** The emigration target list handed the searcher whatever form the tree held, which in these parishes is the **Latin of the baptismal entry**. Tested against the index the same hour:

| | |
|---|---|
| `firstname=josip` | returns records |
| `firstname=joseph` | returns records |
| **`firstname=josephus`** | **0** |
| `firstname=giuseppe` | **0** |

**And the site's own «include name variants» box is on by default and still returns nothing for Josephus**, so whatever it expands, it does not expand across the languages a Croatian parish was written in. **Josephus is the form the target list was handing people.**

**The archive had the answer the whole time.** `tools/given_names.py` has folded the forms into groups since the first week and **no search has ever consulted it**. What was missing was not the grouping but the **language** — because the question a searcher asks is not «what else was he called» but «what would the clerk in *this* index have written».

---

**What was built.** `sources/givennames.psv` — every form, by language — and `tools/names.py`, which marks a form **attested** only if the records contain it and **refuses to build** if a form the records hold is missing from the table. **39 names, 340 forms, 159 attested.** Published at [/your-name/](/your-name/), with `?n=` deep links.

**The gate found three things on its first three runs, and they are the point of the row.**

* **Two men called Mathæus** were sitting outside the group of twenty-one Matijas they belong to, **separated by a single «t»** — `matthaeus` was in the fold table and `mathaeus` was not. The same disease as the surname fold that split on a bracket but not a slash.
* **The table was built from the men.** Every group with a Latin feminine — *Joanna, Josepha, Georgia, Jacoba, Paulina* — had nowhere to put her, so **eight Joannas, two Josephas, two Georgias and a Jacoba fell out of the fold entirely**, and out of every variant list built from it. That is the worst place for a hole: the women of this tree are already its weakest part, seven direct ancestors carrying no surname at all. Five feminine groups added. **And it incidentally folds `pava` to `Paulina`** — the Boras entered twice that [row 40](/worklist/) had to find without a name key at all.
* **The sex is counted now, not asserted.** The fold declares `matija` a man's name; **eight of its forty bearers here are women**, one of them **ahnentafel 13, Matia Pilipić**, whose marriage is [row 4](/worklist/). Croatian Matija is unisex and the table had one column for it.

---

**And the target list is a tool now.** It said of itself that it was *«generated from the archive rather than typed, so it cannot drift from the tree»* — **and nothing generated it.** `tools/fmptargets.py` writes `sources/findmypast/targets.psv`: the same 386 people, plus a **given forms to try** column ordered vernacular and English first because the index on the other end is American or Australian, and Latin last. **305 of the 386 now carry one**; 80 do not, and that is recorded as a gap in the table rather than as a claim that the name has no other forms.

**Latin case endings are never offered.** *Gregorium* is grammar — «baptizavi Gregorium» — not a name anybody was called or indexed under, and **ten rows of the old list named a person that way**.
